name: Ismailism
scope: Ismailism as the defining sources present it: the branch of Shi'i Islam that follows Ismail, eldest son of the sixth imam Ja'far al-Sadiq, as his successor, centred on the doctrine of a living, hereditary imam who gives authoritative teaching (ta'lim) and esoteric interpretation (ta'wil) of the Qur'an (SAET, IIS, IEP). It covers the medieval Fatimid-era thought and state (the da'wa, the codified Ismaili law of al-Qadi al-Nu'man, the Neoplatonist da'is al-Sijistani, al-Kirmani and Nasir Khusraw), the Nizari Alamut state and its later imams, and the two surviving branches, the Nizari (Aga Khan imams, the Ismaili Constitution and the modernising institutions of the Imamat) and the Tayyibi Musta'lian. It does not take in the Druze, who separated from it, nor Twelver or Zaydi Shi'ism, nor the Qarmatians or other extinct splinters except as the sources describe them as Ismaili history.

keyFigures.role: Forty-ninth hereditary imam of the Nizari Ismailis, builder of the Aga Khan Development Network
keyFigures.quote: Shah Karim al-Husayni, Aga Khan IV.

keyFigures.role: Forty-eighth imam of the Nizari Ismailis, who reorganised the community and first gave it a constitution
keyFigures.quote: Aga Khan III (1302–1376/1885–1957), led the Nizārīs as their forty-eighth imām for seventy-two years

keyFigures.role: Founder of the Nizari Ismaili state at Alamut and restater of the doctrine of ta'lim
keyFigures.quote: Ḥasan-i Ṣabbāḥ, who preached the Ismāʿīlī daʿwa on behalf of the Fāṭimids within the Saljūq dominions, had emerged as the undisputed leader of the Persian Ismāʿīlīs.

keyFigures.role: Foremost Fatimid jurist who codified Ismaili law
keyFigures.quote: resulted mainly from the efforts of al-Qāḍī al-Nuʿmān, the foremost Fāṭimid jurist.

keyFigures.role: Fatimid-era Ismaili theologian-philosopher of the imamate
keyFigures.quote: Ḥamīd al-Dīn al-Kirmānī (d. after 411/1020), the most learned Ismāʿīlī theologian-philosopher of the Fāṭimid period

keyFigures.role: Persian poet, traveller and da'i, the best-known Ismaili writer in Persian
keyFigures.quote: As Nasir Khusraw, the best known of the Ismaili writers in Persian

keyFigures.role: Ismaili Neoplatonist da'i of the tenth century
keyFigures.quote: Abū Yaʿqūb al-Sijistānī (d. after 361/971), had set about harmonizing their Ismāʿīlī theology

summary: Ismailism is the Shi'i Muslim tradition that follows Ismail son of Ja'far al-Sadiq and holds that a living, hereditary imam from the Prophet's line gives authoritative teaching and the esoteric interpretation of the Qur'an. It has a cyclical view of sacred history and a philosophical and legal tradition from the Fatimid era, and today the Nizari community is organised under the Aga Khan's Imamat and a constitution that separates spiritual allegiance to the imam from citizens' secular allegiance. Its sources give few positions on contested political questions: they stress freedom of belief, human dignity, women's participation and service to the needy.
